section: Prerequisites / Why this matters for ML
question: Why is a pretraining data loader considered one of the most invisible sources of training bugs?
options: If the (x, y) shift is off or documents bleed together, the model silently learns the wrong objective
It is the only component that runs custom CUDA kernels, so any indexing error crashes the entire GPU process
It rebuilds the model architecture every epoch, so a bad batch silently changes the layer count
It owns the learning-rate schedule, so a wrong batch count makes the optimizer diverge mid-run
explanation: The data loader is called every training step. If the target shift is wrong or documents bleed into each other, nothing crashes — the model just learns the wrong objective and you chase a mysteriously bad loss for days.

section: Prerequisites / Why this matters for ML
question: In next-token pretraining, how are the input x and target y of a batch related?
options: y is an independent random window drawn from elsewhere in the stream
y is x reversed in time, so the model learns to predict in both directions
y is the document label of x, one class id per window
They are the same slice of the token stream, shifted by one position
explanation: The input x and target y are the same slice of the stream shifted by one position, so y[t] is the token that follows x[t]. That shift is the entire supervision signal for pretraining. Random or reversed targets would teach nothing useful.

section: 1. Intuition: from a pile of documents to training windows
question: What three jobs turn a pile of tokenized documents into pretraining batches?
options: Sort documents by length, pad each one to the longest with zeros, and shuffle the padded rows every epoch
Remove stop words, lowercase all text, and deduplicate repeated sentences before tokenizing
Mark document boundaries, pack all ids into one stream, cut fixed-length windows with a one-step shift
Split documents into sentences, label each sentence by topic, and batch together sentences with one label
explanation: Three jobs stand between raw documents and the model: mark boundaries (so documents do not run into each other), pack (concatenate all ids into one long 1-D array), and cut windows of length block_size paired with the same window shifted one step.

section: 1. Intuition: from a pile of documents to training windows
question: Why must pretraining mark the boundary between documents?
options: Otherwise the tokenizer cannot decode the stream back into separate documents
Otherwise the model learns to run one article straight into an unrelated one
Otherwise the concatenated stream overflows the model's fixed context window
Otherwise the embedding table ends up with too few rows for the merged documents
explanation: Without a boundary, concatenated documents look like one continuous text, so the model learns spurious continuations from one article into the next. Marking boundaries gives it an explicit 'document over' signal. The tokenizer and context window are unaffected.

section: 1. Intuition: from a pile of documents to training windows
question: What is the advantage of packing documents into one long 1-D stream of ids?
options: Each document keeps its own fixed-length row, simplifying masking
No padding and no wasted space — every token is training signal
Short documents are automatically discarded
The model sees each document only once per epoch in order
explanation: Packing concatenates every document's ids into one stream, so there is no padding and every token contributes to the loss. Padding-based batching would waste compute on pad tokens.

section: 1. Intuition: from a pile of documents to training windows
question: In the pretraining data pipeline, what is block_size?
options: The model's fixed context length T, the length of each training window
The number of separate documents packed into each training batch of windows
The number of raw bytes stored for each token id in the stream
The size of the tokenizer's vocabulary, including special tokens
explanation: block_size (written T) is the model's fixed context length. The packed stream is sliced into T-length windows, each paired with the same window shifted one step right. The batch size and vocabulary size are separate quantities.

question: What is a special token?
options: A byte value that UTF-8 never produces, so it can safely mark boundaries inside the raw stream
The learned merge that occurs more often than any other, promoted to a fixed reserved id after training
A token that the loss function always masks out, so the model never learns to predict it
A reserved vocabulary id that does not stand for any byte or subword and carries structural meaning
explanation: A special token is an id in the vocabulary with structural, not lexical, meaning — it does not stand for any byte or subword. The most fundamental pretraining example is <|endoftext|>, the document separator.

question: What is <|endoftext|> in GPT-2-style pretraining?
options: A marker placed at the start of every sentence so the model knows a new clause begins
The padding token used to fill short documents up to block_size before batching
The end-of-text separator placed between documents to signal 'this document is over'
The token that replaces out-of-vocabulary words the byte-level tokenizer cannot encode
explanation: <|endoftext|> is GPT-2's name for the end-of-text separator. It is placed between documents so the model sees an explicit end-of-document signal. Byte-level BPE has no OOV, so it is not an unknown-word token, and packing uses no padding.

question: If 'The cat sat.' and 'Quantum error correction…' are concatenated without a separator, what does the model learn?
options: Nothing harmful, because the tokenizer inserts a document boundary automatically
To ignore the second document entirely, since its topic is unrelated to the first one shown
To predict 'Quantum' as the natural continuation of 'The cat sat.' — a nonsense dependency
To translate the first document into the second, treating the two as a parallel sentence pair
explanation: Without a separator, the training target after 'The cat sat.' is 'Quantum', so the model is trained to predict a nonsense cross-document continuation and wastes capacity on it. The tokenizer inserts nothing automatically.

question: Because the causal mask still lets attention look back across an <|endoftext|> boundary, what does the model learn about that token?
options: That tokens before <|endoftext|> must be copied verbatim after it
That <|endoftext|> means 'reset — a new document starts now'
That <|endoftext|> should never be predicted, only consumed as input
That attention must be fully blocked across every document boundary
explanation: Attention can still see across the boundary, so the model learns <|endoftext|> as a reset signal: what follows is a fresh, independent document. This is exactly what lets a trained model stop generating at the end of a sample.

question: Why does including <|endoftext|> in training let a model stop generating?
options: The model learns to emit the end-of-text token where documents end, giving an explicit stop signal
Generation always stops automatically once exactly block_size new tokens have been sampled
The token resets the model's weights to their initial values, which cleanly ends the current generated sample
The decoder deletes every token generated after the first repeated phrase it detects
explanation: Having seen <|endoftext|> at every document end, the model learns to predict it when a sample is complete. Emitting it is the explicit 'document over' signal that ends generation. It does not touch weights.

question: Which additional special tokens do chat models add beyond <|endoftext|>?
options: One token per supported language
Separate tokens for each digit 0–9
A token for every punctuation mark
Role markers and turn boundaries
explanation: Chat models add more special tokens such as role markers and turn boundaries to structure conversations; the course builds those in Module 14. Digits and punctuation are ordinary byte/subword tokens.

question: If a BPE tokenizer has V ordinary tokens, how is the <|endoftext|> id typically added?
options: Reuse id 0, replacing the null byte, so the vocabulary size and both tables stay at exactly V rows each
Map it onto the most frequent merged token, so it inherits an already well-trained embedding
Store it outside the vocabulary as a string flag, so it has no embedding row or output logit
Reserve one more id, e.g. V itself, so the embedding table and output head each get an extra row
explanation: You reserve one extra id (say V) for <|endoftext|>, so the model's embedding table and output head both have one more row for it. It is a real vocabulary id with its own embedding, not a reused byte or an out-of-vocabulary marker.

section: 3. Packing: one corpus, one id stream
question: What does pack_documents(list_of_id_lists, eot_id) do?
options: Pads every document to the same length with eot_id and stacks them into a 2-D tensor
Inserts eot_id only between the first and the last document, leaving the middle ones joined directly
Concatenates every document's ids into one stream with eot_id appended after each document
Replaces the most frequent id in each document with eot_id to mark where it ends
explanation: pack_documents extends a list with each document's ids and appends eot_id after every document, then returns the stream as a 1-D torch.long tensor. It does not pad; eot_id follows every document, including the last.

section: 3. Packing: one corpus, one id stream
question: What is pack_documents([[10, 11, 12], [20, 21]], eot_id=0)?
explanation: Each document is followed by eot_id 0, so the result is [10, 11, 12, 0, 20, 21, 0], a 1-D tensor of length 3 + 1 + 2 + 1 = 7. The two zeros are the boundaries. The separator goes after each document, not before.

section: 3. Packing: one corpus, one id stream
question: Why do token-id tensors use dtype torch.long?
options: Token ids index the embedding table, and PyTorch's embedding lookup requires an integer index type
long is the fastest dtype for matrix multiplication on GPUs, so the lookups can run directly on tensor cores
Token ids can be negative after packing, which requires a signed 64-bit floating-point type
long uses less memory per element than uint8, which matters for multi-gigabyte corpora
explanation: Ids index the embedding table, and PyTorch's embedding lookup (and cross-entropy target) require an integer index type; long (64-bit) is the dtype every id tensor uses in the course. Float ids would be meaningless as indices.

section: 3. Packing: one corpus, one id stream
question: How are very large pretraining corpora stored in practice?
options: Ids are streamed to a memory-mapped uint16 file on disk and opened with np.memmap for training
The whole corpus is held as one Python list of ints in RAM and sliced into windows each step
Each document is stored as a separate float32 tensor kept resident on the GPU throughout training
Ids are stored as JSON text files and re-parsed into tensors at the start of every training step
explanation: Real corpora are too large for a Python list. Documents are streamed through the tokenizer and ids written to a memory-mapped uint16 file, then np.memmap lets the OS page in only the windows you touch. The packing logic is identical.

section: 3. Packing: one corpus, one id stream
question: Why is uint16 enough to store token ids for a GPT-2-sized vocabulary on disk?
options: Token ids are always below 256
uint16 stores floats with enough precision for ids
The embedding table is limited to 16 columns
A vocabulary under 65,536 entries fits in 16 bits
explanation: uint16 holds integers 0..65,535, so any vocabulary under 65,536 (like GPT-2's 50,257) fits, halving storage versus 32-bit. Ids go above 255 once merges exist, so 8 bits would not suffice.

section: 3. Packing: one corpus, one id stream
question: What does np.memmap give a pretraining data loader?
options: Automatic placement of the whole dataset in GPU memory before the first training step
Built-in shuffling of documents at every epoch, so get_batch can read windows in order
The OS pages in only the windows actually touched, so the full corpus never has to fit in RAM
Compression of the stored ids to 4 bits each, shrinking the corpus file on disk roughly fourfold
explanation: A memory-mapped file is accessed like an array, but the OS loads only the disk pages for the windows read. With memmap the main cost of a batch is the pages faulted in. It does not move data to GPU, shuffle, or compress.

question: For a pretraining window x, how is the target window y defined?
options: y[t] = x[t-1] — x slid one step to the right
y[t] = x[t+1] — x slid one step to the left
y[t] = x[t] — the same window
y[t] = x[T-1-t] — the window reversed
explanation: At every position t the model must predict the token that actually comes next, so y[t] = x[t+1]. Using y = x would train the model to predict tokens it can already see.

question: How many next-token prediction problems does one length-T training window supply?
options: 1 — only the final position of each window is supervised by the loss term
T — position 0 predicts token 1, position 1 predicts token 2, and so on
T^2 — every pair of positions forms a separate prediction problem
T/2 — only even positions get a target, so windows never overlap
explanation: Each of the T positions has a target, so one window gives T prediction problems at once. The causal mask ensures position t uses only tokens at positions ≤ t, so this is not cheating.

question: What guarantees that position t in a training window cannot peek at its own target?
options: The causal mask, which lets position t use only tokens at positions ≤ t
The <|endoftext|> token, which hides every future token from attention
Random sampling of window start positions, so targets are never adjacent
The torch.long dtype of the id tensor, which blocks reading ahead
explanation: The causal attention mask blocks position t from attending to later positions, so it cannot see token t+1, its target. Without it, supervising all T positions at once would be trivial cheating.

question: How many consecutive tokens from the stream are needed to build one (x, y) training example of length T?
options: T — x and y are exactly the same T tokens of the stream
2T — x and y are two disjoint consecutive windows of T tokens each
T − 1 — the last token of each window is dropped from both
T + 1 — the first T are x and the last T, offset by one, are y
explanation: x is data[i : i+T] and y is data[i+1 : i+1+T], so together they span T + 1 consecutive tokens. Forgetting the extra token is the root of off-by-one errors.

question: In get_batch, why is high = data.numel() - block_size?
options: It reserves the final block_size tokens of the stream as a held-out validation set that training never sees
It makes the largest start exactly N - block_size, so the very last window of the stream is sampled twice as often
randint's high is exclusive, so the largest start is N - block_size - 1, where x and shifted y still fit
It ensures every sampled start index is a multiple of block_size, so windows never overlap one another
explanation: The target slice data[i+1 : i+1+block_size] reads up to index i + block_size, so we need i ≤ N − block_size − 1. Since randint's high is exclusive, high = N − block_size makes the max draw exactly that. Off by one wastes the last window or indexes past the end.

question: What does data.numel() return for the 1-D packed token stream?
options: The number of documents packed into the stream
The number of distinct token ids that appear in it
The number of elements, i.e. the stream's length N
The size of the stream in bytes, i.e. 8 bytes per id
explanation: numel() returns the total number of elements in a tensor; for a 1-D id stream that is just its length N. It does not count documents, distinct ids, or bytes.

question: What does ix = torch.randint(low=0, high=high, size=(batch_size,)) produce in get_batch?
options: A (batch_size, block_size) tensor of random token ids drawn from the vocabulary
A 1-D int64 tensor of shape (batch_size,) with uniform random start positions in [0, high)
A single random integer that is used as the start position for every row of the batch
A float tensor of probabilities over start positions, later sampled from with torch.multinomial
explanation: torch.randint returns int64 values uniformly from [0, high), here batch_size of them, one start per row. Sampling indices, not data, is nearly free and lets get_batch slice views from the one big tensor.

question: Why does get_batch draw random window starts rather than sweeping through the stream in order?
options: Random starts make successive batches near-independent, so consecutive gradients are not highly correlated
Sequential sweeps would need the entire stream resident in GPU memory, which exceeds capacity at scale
Random starts guarantee that every token is seen exactly once per epoch, unlike sequential sweeps
torch.stack only accepts slices taken in random order, so a sequential sweep raises an error
explanation: Marching through the stream in order gives consecutive batches from adjacent text, so gradients are highly correlated and training less stable. Random starts make batches near-independent. They do not guarantee exactly-once coverage.

question: Why does get_batch sample start indices instead of shuffling the data itself?
options: Shuffling the stream in place would silently convert it from torch.long to a float dtype
Index tensors can be sent to the GPU, but the packed data tensor itself is pinned to the CPU
Shuffling would remove the <|endoftext|> separators, since they are sorted to the end of the stream
A handful of integers is almost free and lets it slice views from the one big tensor without copying
explanation: Drawing batch_size integers is trivially cheap, and slicing data[i : i+block_size] gives views into the existing tensor. Shuffling a giant array would be expensive and would also destroy the contiguous order windows depend on.

question: In get_batch, what shape does torch.stack produce from batch_size slices each of shape (block_size,)?
options: (batch_size * block_size,), concatenated end to end
(block_size, batch_size), along a new trailing axis
(batch_size, block_size, 1), with an extra singleton axis
(batch_size, block_size), along a new leading axis
explanation: torch.stack joins tensors along a new dimension 0, giving (batch_size, block_size). torch.cat would instead concatenate the windows end to end into one 1-D tensor, which is why stack is used.

question: In get_batch, how do the slices and the stacked batch differ in memory?
options: Both the slices and the stacked batch are views into data, so no memory is allocated per batch
The slices are copies of data, while torch.stack returns a view that stitches those copies together
The slices are views into data, while torch.stack allocates a new contiguous tensor independent of it
Both are fresh copies, so each call temporarily doubles memory compared with the stream itself
explanation: Basic slicing data[i : i+block_size] returns a view sharing storage with data. torch.stack allocates a new tensor, so the batch is contiguous and independent of the stream.

question: Why must get_batch reuse the same ix for building y as for x?
options: Reusing ix halves the random-number generation cost, but drawing a fresh ix for y would work equally well
So y[b, t] = data[i+1+t] = x[b, t+1]; fresh random starts would make targets unrelated to inputs
torch.randint can only be called once per batch, since a second call resets the global generator state
Drawing a new ix for y would change its dtype from torch.long to int32, breaking cross-entropy
explanation: x[b] and y[b] come from the same start i, so y[b, t] = data[i+1+t] and x[b, t] = data[i+t], giving y[b, t] == x[b, t+1]. If y used different random starts, the targets would have nothing to do with the inputs and the model would learn nothing.

question: Why does get_batch do its indexing on the CPU and call .to(device) only at the end?
options: Integer bookkeeping is cheap on CPU, and moving only finished batches avoids forcing the stream onto the GPU
GPUs cannot index tensors with integer index tensors, so every slice has to be computed on the CPU first
torch.stack is not implemented for CUDA tensors, so the batch must be stacked on the CPU before transfer
Calling .to(device) before slicing would silently change the dtype of the stream from long to float32
explanation: The slicing and stacking are cheap integer work on CPU; only the two finished (B, T) batches are transferred to the compute device. Threading device through as an argument avoids putting the entire data stream on the GPU up front. If device is 'cpu', .to('cpu') is effectively a no-op.

question: Which two guard clauses does the real get_batch in llmre.data.loader add, and why?
options: That data is 1-D and that data.numel() > block_size, because both failures are otherwise silent or opaque
That data is float32 and that batch_size is even, because odd batches break the stacking logic
That the device is CUDA and that block_size is a power of two, because randint needs an aligned range
That every document ends with eot_id and that ids are sorted, because packing assumes sorted input
explanation: A 2-D data tensor would make the slices mean the wrong thing silently, and a stream no longer than block_size gives high ≤ 0, which torch.randint rejects with an opaque error. Failing early with a clear message is cheaper than debugging symptoms.

question: What vectorized alternative to the Python loop builds a get_batch batch in one indexing op?
options: x = data.view(batch_size, block_size) and y = x.roll(1) over the time dimension
x = data[ix] and y = data[ix + 1], gathering one token per row of the batch
x = torch.cat([data[ix]] * block_size) and y = x + 1, broadcast over every position
idx = ix[:, None] + torch.arange(block_size), then x = data[idx] and y = data[idx + 1]
explanation: Broadcasting ix[:, None] + arange(block_size) gives a (batch_size, block_size) index matrix; gathering data[idx] and data[idx + 1] yields x and y in one fused op, faster on GPU since it launches one kernel instead of batch_size slice-and-stack steps.

question: With data = torch.arange(12), block_size = 4, if a row of x is [4, 5, 6, 7], what is the matching row of y?
explanation: y is x shifted one token: from start i = 4, x = data[4:8] = [4, 5, 6, 7] and y = data[5:9] = [5, 6, 7, 8]. Position 0 sees 4 and predicts 5; position 1 sees 4, 5 and predicts 6.

question: What one-line sanity check confirms a pretraining data loader's targets are correctly shifted?
options: torch.equal(x, y) returns True for the whole batch
torch.equal(x[:, 1:], y[:, :-1]) returns True
torch.equal(x[:, :-1], y[:, 1:]) returns True
x.sum() == y.sum() for every row of the batch
explanation: If y is x shifted left by one, then every target except the last equals the next input: y[:, :-1] == x[:, 1:]. Run this boolean whenever you touch a data loader. torch.equal(x, y) being True would indicate the unshifted bug.

question: What symptom indicates the classic data-loader off-by-one y = data[i : i + block_size]?
options: Training loss stays exactly constant from the first step, as if the gradients were all zero
Training loss plummets to near zero within a few steps while the model learns nothing useful
The loss becomes NaN immediately on the first backward pass because the targets overflow
The model quickly collapses to predicting only <|endoftext|> at every single position
explanation: Without the +1, y equals x, so the model is trained to predict a token it can already see — trivial to fit. A suspiciously low training loss in the first few steps almost always means the targets are not shifted.

question: What are the shape and dtype of the packed token stream in the pretraining pipeline?
options: (N,), torch.long — the whole corpus with documents joined by eot_id
(B, T), torch.long — one fixed-length row per original document
(N, C), torch.float32 — every token already looked up in the embedding
(N,), torch.float16 — ids normalized to [0, 1] by the vocabulary size
explanation: The packed stream is a 1-D long tensor of length N containing every document's ids separated by eot_id. Batches cut from it are (B, T). Embeddings (B, T, C) come later in the model.

question: What are the shape and dtype of a pretraining batch x and its target y?
options: x is (B, T) long and y is (B,) long
x is (B, T, C) float32 and y is (B, T) long
Both (T, B) with dtype torch.float32
Both (B, T) with dtype torch.long
explanation: x holds B input windows of length T = block_size, and y holds the same windows shifted one token left, so both are (B, T) long. y supplies one target per position, not one per window.

question: Where do x and y go after get_batch returns them?
options: x goes to the cross-entropy loss as the target, and y is looked up in the embedding table
Both are embedded to (B, T, C) and concatenated along the channel axis before the first layer
x enters the embedding table, (B, T) → (B, T, C); y is the target for the cross-entropy loss
x is decoded back into text for logging, and y is discarded once the batch has been validated
explanation: The input ids x are looked up in the embedding table to become (B, T, C) activations, and y is passed as the integer target to cross-entropy. y is never embedded.

section: 6. Under the hood: why random windows, and the cost
question: What is the cost of one get_batch call, and how does it compare to training?
options: O(N) per call because it scans the whole stream to find document boundaries before sampling starts
O(N log N) per call because it sorts the stream by token id before drawing the window start positions
O(B · T) memory copies, negligible next to the forward/backward pass, so re-sampling each step is fine
O(B · T^2) per call because it computes causal attention over each window before returning it
explanation: get_batch draws B random integers and gathers B windows of length T, so its cost is O(B · T) copies — negligible next to the model's forward and backward pass. With a memmap, the only real cost is the disk pages the OS faults in.

section: 6. Under the hood: why random windows, and the cost
question: What mild side benefit comes from sampling window starts uniformly over the stream?
options: Every document is guaranteed to appear in exactly one batch per epoch, so coverage is perfectly even
A token is seen in many different context alignments, with window boundaries in different places
Rare tokens are automatically oversampled relative to common ones, which balances the vocabulary
The model never sees an <|endoftext|> token at a window boundary, so documents are never split
explanation: Because starts are uniform, a given token lands at different positions with different preceding context across an epoch, and window boundaries fall in different places. That is a mild, free form of data augmentation. It does not guarantee coverage or rebalance tokens.

question: For data = torch.arange(100), what are the shapes and dtype of x and y from get_batch(data, block_size=8, batch_size=16)?
options: Both (16, 8) with dtype torch.long
Both (8, 16) with dtype torch.long
x is (16, 8) and y is (16, 9), dtype torch.long
Both (16, 8) with dtype torch.float32
explanation: get_batch returns batch_size windows of length block_size for both x and y, so (16, 8). torch.arange of integers is int64 and slicing preserves it, so the dtype is torch.long.

question: For data = torch.arange(100) and block_size = 8, what is the largest start index get_batch can sample?
options: 92, since high = 100 − 8 = 92 is inclusive for torch.randint
99, the last valid index of the stream, since y can wrap around
88, the last multiple of block_size that fits before the end of the stream
91, since high = 92 is exclusive and y = data[92:100] ends at the last token
explanation: high = numel − block_size = 92 is the exclusive upper bound for torch.randint, so the max start is 91. Then x = data[91:99] and y = data[92:100], ending at index 99. A start of 92 would need index 100, which does not exist.

question: Is <|endoftext|> just a string marker, or a real part of the model?
options: It is a text marker that the tokenizer strips out before training, so no id is ever stored
It is a hard-coded rule in the sampler that halts generation, not an entry in the vocabulary
It is a byte sequence that BPE splits into ordinary tokens like any other piece of text
It is a real vocabulary id with its own embedding that the model can predict and emit
explanation: The separator is a reserved vocabulary id with its own embedding row and output logit. The model learns to predict it at document ends, which provides the 'document over' signal used to stop generation.

question: Given x[0] = [4, 5, 6, 7] and correctly shifted targets, what does position 2 see and predict?
options: It sees 4, 5, 6, 7 and is trained to predict 8, the next token after the window
It sees only 6, its own position, and is trained to predict 7
It sees 4, 5, 6 (the causal mask blocks 7) and is trained to predict 7
It sees 4, 5 (the mask blocks its own token) and is trained to predict 6
explanation: y[0] = [5, 6, 7, 8], so the target at position 2 is y[0][2] = 7. The causal mask lets position 2 attend only to positions 0–2 (tokens 4, 5, 6), so it cannot see 7, its answer.

question: A model reaches a training loss near 0 within 10 steps on real text. What is the single most likely bug?
options: The learning rate is far too low, so the optimizer barely moves the weights
The targets are not shifted — y equals x (or is shifted the wrong way)
The tokenizer vocabulary is too small, so every token becomes easy to guess
The batch size is too large, so each gradient step averages away the noise
explanation: Real text cannot be predicted near-perfectly in 10 steps. The likely cause is y equal to x, so the model 'predicts' a token it can already see. Check torch.equal(x[:, 1:], y[:, :-1]).

question: Why would float32 token ids be wrong in PyTorch?
options: Embedding lookup and the cross-entropy target both need integer (long) indices, so floats are a type error
float32 cannot represent integers above 65,535 exactly, so ids from large vocabularies get corrupted
float32 ids would make training noticeably slower on GPUs but would still give exactly correct results
float32 ids are automatically rounded during lookup, which causes off-by-one errors near large ids
explanation: Token ids are integer indices into the embedding table. nn.Embedding and cross-entropy's target argument both require an integer index type, so passing floats is both meaningless and a type error.
